title: 22. Interview: Kubernetes (Cloud Deployment)
summary: Interview Q&A for Kubernetes (Cloud Deployment) — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Kubernetes (Cloud Deployment) interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What problem does managed Kubernetes solve versus self-hosted Kubernetes?
**Answer:** Self-hosted Kubernetes forces you to operate etcd (the cluster's source of truth), the API server, scheduler, controller manager, and the kubelet on every node. You handle certificate rotation, version upgrades, etcd backups, control-plane HA across AZs, and security patching — a workload that typically requires a dedicated SRE team. Managed Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS) offloads the control plane to the provider, who runs it multi-AZ, handles upgrades, and exposes an API endpoint you authenticate to via cloud IAM. You still manage node pools, workloads, and add-ons, but the most fragile components are operated for you. The trade-off is the per-cluster fee (EKS ~$73/month), enforced upgrade cadences (typically 14 months), and limits on certain configuration knobs. For most teams the math favors managed K8s because the operational burden of self-hosting exceeds the cost, and because cloud IAM integration, integrated logging, and provider-managed CSI/CNI plugins save real engineering time.
**Visual:**
```
self-hosted:  you run [etcd][apiserver][sched][cm][kubelets] x N nodes
managed:      provider runs [etcd][apiserver][sched][cm]  you run [kubelets] x N
```

### Q2. How does the Cluster Autoscaler decide when to add or remove nodes?
**Answer:** The Cluster Autoscaler (CA) is a controller that watches for Pods in the Pending state — Pods the scheduler could not place because no node has enough allocatable CPU, memory, GPU, or extended resources. When CA sees Pending Pods, it simulates scheduling them on a hypothetical new node in each node pool, picks the pool that would let them fit, and calls the cloud provider's API (e.g., AWS Auto Scaling Groups) to add a node. After the node registers with the control plane, the normal scheduler places the Pending Pods. Scale-down is more conservative: CA marks nodes as underutilized only if their total requested resources fall below a threshold (default 50%) for a sustained period (default 10 minutes), and it only drains a node if all its Pods can be rescheduled elsewhere — system-critical Pods, local-storage Pods, and Pods not backed by a controller are not displaced. This conservatism prevents flapping but means scale-down lags behind load reduction.
**Visual:**
```
Pending Pods -> CA simulates scheduling on +1 node per pool
            -> picks pool that fits -> cloud API adds node
underused node (cpu<50% for 10m, Pods safely movable) -> drain + remove
```

### Q3. What is the difference between a Service, an Ingress, and a Service Mesh?
**Answer:** A Service is a Kubernetes abstraction that gives a stable virtual IP and DNS name to a set of Pods, load-balancing traffic across them using kube-proxy iptables/IPVS rules. A Service of type ClusterIP is reachable only inside the cluster; NodePort exposes a port on every node; LoadBalancer provisions one cloud TCP load balancer per Service, which is expensive if you have many services. An Ingress is an L7 resource that lets one cloud load balancer route to many Services based on HTTP host and path, implemented by an Ingress controller (nginx-ingress, AWS Load Balancer Controller, Traefik). A Service Mesh (Istio, Linkerd, App Mesh) operates at a different layer: it injects a sidecar proxy into every Pod to provide mTLS, traffic shaping (retries, timeouts, circuit breaking), canary splits, and observability for east-west traffic between services. Ingress handles north-south traffic from outside the cluster; mesh handles east-west traffic inside.
**Visual:**
```
internet -> Ingress (ALB, host/path routing) -> Service (ClusterIP)
                                                      |
                                          +-----+-----+-----+
                                          |Pod  |Pod  |Pod  |  each with
                                          +sidecar (mesh) ----+ mTLS + traces
```

### Q4. Why run multiple node pools instead of one big pool?
**Answer:** Different workloads have different requirements that one pool cannot satisfy cost-effectively. Stateful services and latency-sensitive APIs need on-demand instances that will not be reclaimed; background workers can tolerate spot interruptions at one-third the cost; ML inference needs GPU instances; caches and in-memory databases need memory-optimized shapes. A single pool forces you to run everything on the most expensive instance type that satisfies any workload, and it makes node selectors meaningless. Multiple pools let you assign Pods to the right hardware via `nodeSelector` or `nodeAffinity`, and let the cluster autoscaler scale each pool independently. Shopify and Slack both partition EKS/GKE clusters this way: interactive traffic on on-demand pools, batch on spot, ML on GPU. The trade-off is operational complexity — each pool is its own autoscaling group with its own upgrade cadence, and fragmentation can leave a pool underutilized if a workload moves.
**Visual:**
```
one pool:   [m5.4xl x 50]  -> everything runs here, costly
multi-pool: [ondemand m5.2xl x 10]  api, scheduler
            [spot m5.4xl    x 30]  workers, indexers
            [gpu g4dn.xl    x  4]  inference
            [mem r5.2xl     x  6]  redis, memcached
```

### Q5. What is a cold-start-like issue in Kubernetes and how is it mitigated?
**Answer:** Kubernetes itself does not have function cold starts, but it has analogous scale-up latency. When the cluster autoscaler provisions a new node, the cloud provider must launch the VM (30–90 seconds on AWS, often 1–3 minutes on cold pools), the node must register with the control plane (5–15 seconds), pull the container image (10–60 seconds depending on size and cache), and then start the Pod. Total time from Pending Pod to Running Pod is commonly 60–180 seconds, which is much slower than the function cold start of serverless. Mitigations include: pre-pulling images onto nodes via a DaemonSet so image pull is instant; using GKE's Fast Launch or AWS BottleRocket images that boot faster; keeping spare capacity by setting a higher `minNodes`; using `cluster-autoscaler`'s balance-similar-node-groups feature; and using horizontal Pod autoscaling on CPU/RPS so the HPA scales replicas first within existing capacity, with node scaling only as the backstop. For truly bursty workloads, serverless containers (Cloud Run, Fargate) often outperform K8s.
**Visual:**
```
Pending Pod -> cloud provisions VM (60s) -> register (10s) -> pull image (30s) -> Running
mitigate: pre-pull images, raise minNodes, HPA before CA, use BottleRocket
```

### Q6. How does cloud IAM integrate with Kubernetes RBAC in EKS?
**Answer:** EKS uses IAM authentication via an authenticator that maps AWS IAM principals to Kubernetes identities. The `aws-auth` ConfigMap in the `kube-system` namespace lists which IAM ARNs map to which Kubernetes users or groups, and the API server consults it on every request. When you run `kubectl`, the AWS SDK signs the request with your IAM credentials, EKS validates the signature, looks up the IAM ARN in `aws-auth`, and presents the corresponding K8s identity to RBAC. RBAC rules (`Role`, `RoleBinding`, `ClusterRole`, `ClusterRoleBinding`) then decide whether that identity can perform the requested verb on the requested resource. IAM roles for service accounts (IRSA) extend this to Pods: each Pod can assume an IAM role via OIDC federation, so a Pod in EKS can read from S3 without static credentials. GKE and AKS have analogous integrations (Workload Identity, Azure AD workload identity). This pattern lets you manage cloud and K8s access from one identity provider.
**Visual:**
```
IAM role arn:aws:iam::123:role/dev-team  --(aws-auth ConfigMap)--> group: dev-team
                                                                     |
                                              ClusterRoleBinding: dev-team -> view ClusterRole
```

### Q7. What are the cost trade-offs between EKS, Fargate, and Lambda for a stateless API?
**Answer:** EKS charges a per-cluster control-plane fee (~$73/month) plus the cost of EC2 worker nodes that you run continuously; you also pay for the operational overhead of managing the cluster. At high steady-state load this is the cheapest option because EC2 instances are dense and reserved-instance or savings-plan discounts apply. Fargate removes the node management but charges a per-vCPU-hour and per-GB-hour premium (roughly 20–40% above EC2), making it cost-effective at low to medium scale or for bursty workloads where you cannot keep nodes busy. Lambda charges per request and per GB-second of execution, with no idle cost — ideal for low-volume or spiky event-driven workloads, but at high sustained RPS it becomes the most expensive option and is capped by concurrency limits. A pragmatic pattern is: route low-volume endpoints to Lambda, medium-volume services to Fargate or Cloud Run, and high-volume services to EKS with reserved capacity.
**Visual:**
```
low RPS    : Lambda  $  (pay per call, no idle)
medium RPS : Fargate $$ (per pod-hour, no nodes)
high RPS   : EKS    $$$ per cluster + cheap nodes, best $/req at scale
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your EKS cluster has Pending Pods but the Cluster Autoscaler is not adding nodes. How do you debug?
**Answer:** First, inspect a Pending Pod with `kubectl describe pod <name>` and look at the Events section — the scheduler will say whether it failed for insufficient CPU, insufficient memory, a node selector mismatch, or a taint/toleration problem. If the message is `0/12 nodes are available: 12 Insufficient cpu`, then autoscaling should fire; check `kubectl logs -n kube-system deployment/cluster-autoscaler` for messages like `scale-up: setting group ... size from X to Y`. If CA logs show no scale-up attempt, verify the node group's `maxSize` is not already reached and that the pod's `nodeSelector` matches a pool that exists. If CA tries but the cloud API fails, check IAM permissions for the CA service account, ASG quota, or capacity errors in the cloud's `service-limit` metrics. If `describe` says `node(s) had volume node affinity conflict`, the Pod's PVC is bound to a specific AZ and cannot be placed elsewhere — fix the StorageClass or replicate the data.
**Visual:**
```
kubectl describe pod -> Events:
  Warning FailedScheduling  Insufficient cpu
  -> check CA logs -> maxNodes? nodeSelector match? IAM? ASG quota?
```

### Q2. You run a workload that spikes from 50 to 5000 RPS in under a minute. EKS scaling is too slow. What do you do?
**Answer:** Node provisioning latency (60–180 seconds) cannot meet a sub-minute spike, so you must shift the response curve. First, configure the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler to scale replicas aggressively on RPS or CPU ahead of node pressure — Pods Pending is the trigger for CA, so the faster HPA raises replica count, the faster CA fires. Second, keep spare node capacity by raising `minNodes` or by running a `pause`-container Deployment that occupies reserved capacity and is evicted (via lower priorityClass) when real workloads need the space. Third, pre-pull container images onto nodes via a DaemonSet so new Pods start in seconds instead of waiting on image pulls. Fourth, consider predictive scaling or scheduled scaling if the spike pattern is regular — EKS supports scheduled actions on the underlying ASG. Fifth, front the service with a load balancer that can absorb the burst with queueing and circuit breaking. For genuinely unpredictable sub-minute spikes, serverless containers (Cloud Run, Fargate) or Lambda will outperform EKS because they elide node provisioning entirely.
**Visual:**
```
HPA: replicas 5 -> 80 (RPS-based)        <-- 10s
CA : Pending Pods -> new nodes           <-- 90s
fix: raise minNodes, pre-pull images, reserve capacity with pause pods,
     use scheduled scaling, front with buffering LB
```

### Q3. Your team needs to run a multi-tenant SaaS on EKS. How do you isolate tenants?
**Answer:** Multi-tenant isolation on EKS requires layering several controls. Use Kubernetes Namespaces to give each tenant its own logical boundary, then enforce RBAC so tenant users can only see their own namespace. NetworkPolicies (calico or the AWS VPC CNI policy engine) restrict east-west traffic so a Pod in tenant A cannot reach a Pod in tenant B. ResourceQuotas and LimitRanges prevent any one tenant from consuming the cluster's CPU/memory. For stronger isolation, run each tenant's Pods on dedicated node pools using `nodeSelector` or `nodeAffinity` plus taints and tolerations so no two tenants share a kernel — this is the defense-in-depth pattern against container escapes. For the strongest isolation, run each tenant in a separate EKS cluster (or virtual cluster via vcluster), accepting the cost overhead. At the data layer, encrypt each tenant's data with a per-tenant KMS key via IRSA. The trade-off is always isolation strength versus operational cost: namespace-level is cheap and weak; per-tenant clusters are expensive and strong.
**Visual:**
```
weak:   1 cluster, ns per tenant, NetworkPolicy, ResourceQuota
medium: 1 cluster, dedicated node pool per tenant (taints)
strong: 1 cluster per tenant (or vcluster) + per-tenant KMS keys
```

### Q4. You are migrating a stateful service from EC2 to EKS. What pitfalls do you anticipate?
**Answer:** Stateful workloads challenge the Kubernetes model because Pods are ephemeral but state must persist. The first pitfall is storage: you must use a `StatefulSet` (not Deployment) so each replica gets a stable identity and a dedicated `PersistentVolume` claim via `volumeClaimTemplates`. The second is data replication — if the service was single-node on EC2, moving to a StatefulSet with replicas introduces replication concerns the app may not be designed for; for databases prefer the cloud-managed equivalent (RDS, Cloud SQL) and only run the DB on K8s if you have an operator (e.g., the Postgres operator, Vitess). The third is pod anti-affinity so replicas land on different nodes and AZs; without it, a node failure can take down all replicas. The fourth is graceful shutdown — the Pod's `terminationGracePeriodSeconds` and a `preStop` hook must let the service flush and replicate. The fifth is upgrades — StatefulSet rolling updates are slower and risk data divergence if rushed. Shopify and Slack both keep their databases on managed services, not on EKS.
**Visual:**
```
StatefulSet:  Pod-0 -> PVC-0 -> PV-A (EBS gp3, AZ-a)
              Pod-1 -> PVC-1 -> PV-B (EBS gp3, AZ-b)
              Pod-2 -> PVC-2 -> PV-C (EBS gp3, AZ-c)
   podAntiAffinity: replicas on different nodes/AZs
   preStop hook: flush + resignal replication
```

### Q5. Traffic to one of your services on EKS has 5xx errors spiking intermittently. How do you triangulate?
**Answer:** Start by reducing the layers — client, cloud LB, ingress, service mesh sidecar, application Pod, downstream dependencies — and gather signal from each. Check the AWS ALB access logs (or equivalent) for whether 5xx originate at the ALB (502 = no healthy targets, 504 = timeout) or are passed through from the Pod. Check the ingress controller logs for routing errors. If you run a service mesh, check Envoy access logs — the sidecar adds observability that often reveals whether the error is from the local Pod or an upstream call. Use `kubectl top pods` and `kubectl describe pod` to look for CPU throttling, OOM kills, or restarts; check Pod `kubectl logs` for application errors. Trace a request through distributed tracing (Jaeger, Datadog, X-Ray) to see which hop failed. Common culprits: HPA scaled too slowly and Pods are CPU-throttled under load; a downstream dependency (DB, cache) is saturated; an Ingress annotation is wrong; an mTLS cert in the mesh expired; or a node is unhealthy and kubelet is failing health checks. The mesh makes debugging both harder (extra hop) and easier (rich access logs).
**Visual:**
```
client -> ALB(502? 504?) -> ingress(4xx? 5xx?) -> sidecar(envoy log)
   -> Pod (kubectl logs, top, describe) -> DB/Cache (saturating?)
distributed trace shows which span turned red
```

### Q6. You need to perform a zero-downtime Kubernetes version upgrade on a production EKS cluster. Walk through the plan.
**Answer:** EKS managed upgrades require upgrading the control plane first, then the nodes, then add-ons. Start by reviewing the Kubernetes release notes for breaking changes (deprecated APIs are the main risk — e.g., `networking.k8s.io/v1beta1` removed in 1.22). Run `kubectl convert` or a tool like `pluto` to find deprecated API usage in your manifests. Upgrade add-ons (CSI, CNI, kube-proxy) to versions compatible with the target K8s release. Trigger the control-plane upgrade via the EKS console or API; it takes 15–30 minutes and briefly disrupts API availability per AZ. Once the control plane is upgraded, the nodes are still on the old version — drain and replace them in waves. With managed node groups, use `eksctl upgrade nodegroup --kubernetes-version` or replace nodes via a rolling update; the cluster drains each node respecting PodDisruptionBudgets, so set PDBs to ensure quorum on stateful services. Validate with canary traffic before completing the wave. Slack and Shopify run weekly canary upgrades on staging clusters to catch issues before they hit production. Always keep the previous version's AMI cached so you can roll back.
**Visual:**
```
1. scan manifests for deprecated APIs (pluto)
2. upgrade add-ons (CSI, CNI, kube-proxy)
3. upgrade control plane (15-30 min, per-AZ API blips)
4. upgrade node groups in waves: drain -> replace -> validate
   PodDisruptionBudgets protect quorum
5. canary traffic before completing each wave
```

### Q7. Your CFO wants to cut the EKS bill by 30%. Where do you find the savings?
**Answer:** The biggest EKS cost is the underlying EC2 fleet, so focus there. First, identify idle resources: `kubectl top nodes` and `kubectl top pods` reveal underutilized nodes; tune the cluster autoscaler's scale-down thresholds (lower the `--scale-down-unneeded-time` and `--scale-down-utilization-threshold`) so empty nodes are reclaimed faster. Second, right-size Pods: developers routinely request 1 CPU when they need 100m; the Vertical Pod Autoscaler in recommendation mode reports actual usage and you can lower requests, which lets more Pods pack per node. Third, move stateless, interruptible workloads to spot instances — savings of 60–90% on those node pools; use node selectors and a spot interruption handler to drain gracefully. Fourth, consolidate clusters: each EKS cluster costs ~$73/month for the control plane, so 20 small clusters becomes 4 larger ones saves $14k/year. Fifth, apply Savings Plans or Reserved Instances to the on-demand baseline. Sixth, consider GKE Autopilot or AWS Fargate for low-volume services to eliminate idle node cost. Seventh, audit logging cost — CloudWatch Logs on verbose kube-system logs can be surprisingly expensive; tune retention.
**Visual:**
```
right-size Pod requests  -> pack more Pods per node
spot for stateless       -> -60..90% on those pools
consolidate clusters     -> -control plane fee x N
Savings Plans on baseline -> -30..50% on on-demand
Fargate for low volume   -> eliminate idle nodes
```
